title: Repeat Spreaders and Election Delegitimization: A Comprehensive Dataset of Misinformation Tweets from the 2020 U.S. Election
screen_reason: Reports two quantitative concentration estimates with denominators: the top 35 'repeat spreader' accounts account for a stated 28.6% of all retweets/quote tweets in the election-delegitimizing subset, and the top 150 repeat spreaders account for a stated 50% of all retweets and quote tweets in ElectionMisinfo2020. Both are 'a top group of users accounting for a stated share of sharing' (CONCENTRATION).

estimates.measure_type: % of all retweets and quote tweets in election-delegitimizing ('sows doubt') misinformation stories that came from the top 35 repeat-spreader accounts
estimates.conc_group_label: top 35 'repeat spreader' accounts, ranked by number of distinct 'sows doubt' stories in which they posted an original tweet/quote tweet/reply with >1,000 retweets
estimates.denominator: 32,581,921 retweets and quote tweets connected to the 307 'sows doubt' misinformation stories in ElectionMisinfo2020
estimates.definition: Numerator = retweets and quote tweets tied to original content posted by the 35 highest-ranked repeat-spreader accounts; ranking is by count of distinct election-delegitimizing stories in which the account posted a tweet receiving more than 1,000 retweets.
estimates.misinfo_def: "distinct, time-bounded, informational 'event' encompassing the propagation of a single false, misleading, exaggerated, or unsubstantiated claim or narrative"; "We use the term misinformation for this dataset as an umbrella term, inclusive of rumors, misinformation, and disinformation."
estimates.source_quote: The top 35 accounts alone were responsible for 9,304,879 out of 32,581,921—or 28.6%—of all "sows doubt" connected retweets and quote tweets we collected.
estimates.page_loc: Results, 'Repeat Spreaders' section (p. 24), text accompanying Table 1
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Election Integrity Partnership researchers (112 across 4 organisations) identified misinformation stories in real time (814 reports); stories deduplicated by two independent coders with a third arbitrating; per-story boolean keyword strings validated by an independent coder to a >=90% precision threshold; the 'sows doubt' label applied by at least two coders, Fleiss's Kappa = 0.64, with a three-coder panel arbitrating disagreements.
estimates.moderator_quote: With a team of researchers, we qualitatively coded each of the 456 stories to identify whether the tweets in that story sowed doubt in election procedures or election results. ... After developing the codebook, we had at least two coders code each story. The annotator agreement was substantial (Fleiss's Kappa = 0.64) (Landis and Koch 1977).
estimates.notes: ADJUDICATOR NOTE on conc_group_pct: the paper never states the top 35 as a percentage of accounts. The only account denominator in the text is 'This second step allowed us to mark 1,580,365 accounts, or 57% of all accounts', which implies roughly 2.77 million accounts in ElectionMisinfo2020; 35/2,772,570 = 0.0013%. conc_group_pct is therefore DERIVED from a derived denominator and should be treated as approximate (the conc_share_pct of 28.6% is verbatim). Denominator here is the election-delegitimizing subset (307 of 456 stories, 44.8 million tweets), not the full dataset.

estimates.measure_type: % of all retweets and quote tweets in the ElectionMisinfo2020 dataset that came from the top 150 repeat-spreader accounts
estimates.value_raw: top 150 repeat spreaders "account for 50% of all retweets and quote tweets in ElectionMisinfo2020"
estimates.conc_group_label: top 150 'repeat spreader' accounts (same ranking: distinct 'sows doubt' stories with a >1,000-retweet original tweet)
estimates.denominator: all retweets and quote tweets in ElectionMisinfo2020 (the dataset comprises 49.3 million tweets connected to 456 misinformation stories; the retweet+quote-tweet total is not stated)
estimates.definition: Numerator = retweets and quote tweets that can be tied to an original tweet by one of the 150 highest-ranked repeat-spreader accounts.
estimates.misinfo_def: "distinct, time-bounded, informational 'event' encompassing the propagation of a single false, misleading, exaggerated, or unsubstantiated claim or narrative"
estimates.n: all retweets and quote tweets in ElectionMisinfo2020 (49.3 million tweets in the dataset overall; retweet/quote-tweet subtotal not reported)
estimates.source_quote: However, even at its peak, a relatively small proportion of the tweets, quote tweets and retweets in the Sharpiegate story came from our top 150 repeat spreaders, who account for 50% of all retweets and quote tweets in ElectionMisinfo2020.
estimates.page_loc: Results, 'Sharpiegate' case study (p. 31); corroborated in 'Case Studies' intro (p. 26): "We used 150 accounts because they were also responsible for almost exactly half of the retweets and quote tweets in the data."
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same EIP real-time identification and researcher coding pipeline as the top-35 row; story-level keyword sets validated to >=90% precision by a coder who had not built the search string.
estimates.moderator_quote: We used 150 accounts because they were also responsible for almost exactly half of the retweets and quote tweets in the data.
estimates.notes: Kept as a distinct estimate from the top-35 row: a different group size AND a different denominator (the whole ElectionMisinfo2020 dataset rather than the 'sows doubt' subset). conc_group_pct again DERIVED (150/~2,772,570 accounts implied by '1,580,365 accounts, or 57% of all accounts') and approximate; the 50% share is verbatim. This is the paper's most quotable concentration figure.

missed_or_uncertain: 1) NOT extracted, corpus-wide misinformation prevalence: the broad election-related Twitter collection contains '1.04 Billion tweets' for 1 Sep-15 Dec 2020, and ElectionMisinfo2020 (drawn from it) contains '49.3 million tweets', which would give 4.7%. I did not create a CONTENT row because the numerator does not meet the construct definition: tweets enter ElectionMisinfo2020 by keyword-matching to a misinformation STORY, and the authors state explicitly that 'not all of the tweets linked to a misinformation story are false: some are questions, opinions, corrections, or factual content'. The 4.7% would also be an artefact of how many stories the EIP happened to receive reports about, and the broad collection was rate-limited. Flagging it in case the adjudication rule is to keep derived part/whole shares. 2) NOT extracted: '307 of the 456 misinformation stories' (67.3%) were labelled as sowing doubt in the election - a topical sub-classification inside an all-misinformation corpus, not a veracity share, so R3 (within_misinfo_content) does not apply. 3) NOT extracted: cross-platform link shares among misinformation stories - '192 (62%) of the misinformation stories included at least one tweet with a link to YouTube, 87 (28%) included a link to Facebook, and 61 (20%) linked to Instagram' - denominator is an all-misinformation set and the numerator is a link type, not falsity. 4) NOT extracted: partisan composition of spreaders ('all but two of the top 100 repeat spreader accounts were supporters of then-President Trump'; 'only 11 of those users as Biden supporters' among the top 150) - a demographic/partisan split of the concentrated group, not a prevalence or concentration share. 5) NOT extracted: '31% of the US population still believe the "big lie"' - belief, and cited from PRRI (2021), not this study's data. 6) NOT extracted: daily tweet volumes by partisanship (median 30k/day Trump supporters vs 7.5k/day Biden supporters pre-election) - raw counts with no denominator. 7) NOT extracted: 99.98% capture rate of tweets with >=10 retweets - a data-collection coverage statistic. 8) Table 1 is badly de-linearised in the text extraction (screen names, verified flags, story counts, tweet counts and retweet counts appear as separate runs of numbers); I did not attempt to reconstruct per-account rows from it, and none would be poolable estimates anyway.

rob.design: Non-probability curated platform corpus. Frame: Twitter Streaming API collection of election-related tweets (>160 keywords, multiple collectors, rate-limited; authors estimate 99.98% capture of tweets with >=10 retweets), 1.04 billion tweets for 1 Sep-15 Dec 2020. 814 real-time Election Integrity Partnership reports (79% internal analysts, 21% external collaborators) were qualitatively grouped into 29 content groups by two independent coders with third-coder arbitration, deduplicated, and reduced to 456 distinct stories that spread on Twitter. Each story was mapped to tweets with an iteratively built boolean keyword string; every story was independently validated by someone who had not written the string against a >=90% relevance threshold (random sample plus top-10 retweeted tweets). 'Sows doubt' labelling: at least two coders per story, Fleiss's Kappa = 0.64 (substantial), three-coder arbitration panel; 307 of 456 stories labelled. Partisanship assigned via a coengagement retweet projection network (Louvain clustering; >90% within-cluster tie rule for direct assignment, 80% retweet rule for indirect), covering 57% of accounts and 94% of tweets. Acknowledged limitations: English-only monitoring, analyst/monitoring-topic bias, Twitter-only, and no separation of misinformation-spreading from corrective tweets.
rob.item6_quote: Each misinformation story in ElectionMisinfo2020 reflects a distinct, time-bounded, informational "event" encompassing the propagation of a single false, misleading, exaggerated, or unsubstantiated claim or narrative.
rob.item10_quote: The top 35 accounts alone were responsible for 9,304,879 out of 32,581,921—or 28.6%—of all "sows doubt" connected retweets and quote tweets we collected.
